claims.claim_text: SQLite has offered WAL mode since version 3.7.0.
claims.reasoning: Passage 0 states that beginning with version 3.7.0, a new Write-Ahead Log option is available.

citations.quote: Beginning with version 3.7.0 (2010-07-21), a new "Write-Ahead Log" option (hereafter referred to as "WAL") is available.

claims.claim_text: In WAL mode, writers and readers can run at the same time.
claims.reasoning: Passage 3 directly states writers and readers can run at the same time.

citations.quote: Because writers do nothing that would interfere with the actions of readers, writers and readers can run at the same time.

claims.claim_text: In WAL mode, there can only be one writer at a time.
claims.reasoning: Passage 3 directly states there can only be one writer at a time.

citations.quote: However, since there is only one WAL file, there can only be one writer at a time.

claims.claim_text: A checkpoint runs automatically once the WAL file reaches 1000 pages.
claims.reasoning: Passage 2 states that by default SQLite automatically checkpoints when the WAL file reaches a threshold size of 1000 pages.

citations.quote: By default, SQLite does a checkpoint automatically when the WAL file reaches a threshold size of 1000 pages.

claims.claim_text: The WAL file is normally named after the database file with a "-wal" suffix.
claims.reasoning: Passage 4 states the WAL file name is usually the database file name with an extra "-wal" suffix.

citations.quote: The name of this file on disk is usually the name of the database file with an extra "-wal" suffix

claims.claim_text: WAL works best with smaller transactions.
claims.reasoning: The passage directly states this.

citations.quote: WAL works best with smaller transactions.

claims.claim_text: For transactions larger than about 10 megabytes, the traditional rollback journal modes will likely be faster.
claims.reasoning: The passage says rollback journal modes will likely be faster for transactions larger than about 100 megabytes, not 10 megabytes.

citations.quote: For transactions larger than about 100 megabytes, traditional rollback journal modes will likely be faster.

claims.claim_text: Transactions in excess of a gigabyte may fail with an I/O or disk-full error.
claims.reasoning: The passage states this about WAL mode for transactions over a gigabyte.

citations.quote: For transactions in excess of a gigabyte, WAL mode may fail with an I/O or disk-full error.

claims.claim_text: In applications that mostly read, WAL can be roughly 1% or 2% slower than rollback journaling.
claims.reasoning: The passage says WAL might be slightly slower, perhaps 1% or 2%, in read-mostly applications.

citations.quote: WAL might be very slightly slower (perhaps 1% or 2% slower) than the traditional rollback-journal approach in applications that do mostly reads and seldom write.

claims.claim_text: Write transactions are fast.
claims.reasoning: The passage says write transactions are very fast.

citations.quote: Write transactions are very fast since they only involve writing the content once (versus twice for rollback-journal transactions) and because the writes are all sequential.

claims.claim_text: For write transactions, the content only has to be written once.
claims.reasoning: The passage says write transactions only involve writing the content once.

citations.quote: they only involve writing the content once

claims.claim_text: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers.
claims.reasoning: Passage 0 directly states that a checkpoint can run concurrently with readers.

citations.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers

claims.claim_text: A checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.
claims.reasoning: Passage 0 directly states this requirement.

citations.quote: the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader

claims.claim_text: A long-running read transaction can prevent the checkpointer from making progress.
claims.reasoning: Passage 1 states exactly that a long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.

citations.quote: Thus a long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.

claims.claim_text: If there is always at least one active reader, checkpoints still complete, just more slowly.
claims.reasoning: Passage 3 states that if there is always at least one active reader, no checkpoints will be able to complete, so they do not merely complete more slowly.

citations.quote: However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.claim_text: Running manual checkpoints with SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART guarantees that readers are never blocked.
claims.reasoning: Passage 4 says the disadvantage of SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE is that readers might block while the checkpoint is running, directly conflicting with the claim that readers are never blocked.

citations.quote: The disadvantage of using SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE is that readers might block while the checkpoint is running.

claims.claim_text: Checkpoint starvation is the most common cause of WAL file growth in production systems.
claims.reasoning: The passages describe checkpoint starvation and WAL growth, but they do not state that checkpoint starvation is the most common cause of WAL file growth in production systems.

claims.claim_text: Unlike other journaling modes, WAL journal mode is persistent.
claims.reasoning: The passage directly states that WAL mode is persistent, unlike other journaling modes.

citations.quote: Unlike the other journaling modes, PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL is persistent.

claims.claim_text: If a process sets WAL mode, then closes and reopens the database, the database comes back in WAL mode.
claims.reasoning: The passage states exactly that reopening after setting WAL mode returns in WAL mode.

citations.quote: If a process sets WAL mode, then closes and reopens the database, the database will come back in WAL mode.

claims.claim_text: Applications can be converted to WAL without changing the application itself.
claims.reasoning: The passage says applications can be converted to using SQLite in WAL mode without making changes to the application itself.

citations.quote: The persistence of WAL mode means that applications can be converted to using SQLite in WAL mode without making any changes to the application itself.

claims.claim_text: WAL mode was first released in July 2010.
claims.reasoning: The passages do not mention a release date for WAL mode.

claims.claim_text: WAL mode is the default journal mode for databases created on Android.
claims.reasoning: The passages do not mention Android or default journal modes for databases created on Android.

claims.claim_text: The WAL file should be kept with the database when the database is copied.
claims.reasoning: The passage states the WAL file is part of persistent database state and should be kept if the database is copied or moved.

citations.quote: The WAL file is part of the persistent state of the database and should be kept with the database if the database is copied or moved.

claims.claim_text: The safest way to remove a WAL file is to delete it manually after all processes have stopped.
claims.reasoning: The passage says the only safe way to remove a WAL file is to open and immediately close the database using SQLite interfaces, not to delete it manually.

citations.quote: The only safe way to remove a WAL file is to open the database file using one of the sqlite3_open() interfaces then immediately close the database using sqlite3_close().

claims.claim_text: WAL mode first appeared in SQLite 3.7.0.
claims.reasoning: The passage states that the WAL option became available beginning with version 3.7.0.

citations.quote: Beginning with version 3.7.0 (2010-07-21), a new "Write-Ahead Log" option (hereafter referred to as "WAL") is available.

claims.claim_text: PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL is persistent.
claims.reasoning: The passage explicitly says that journal_mode=WAL is persistent, unlike other journaling modes.

citations.quote: Unlike the other journaling modes, PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL is persistent.

claims.claim_text: Simply closing and reopening a WAL database is not enough to change its page size.
claims.reasoning: The passages say page_size cannot be changed after entering WAL mode and that closing and reopening a WAL database leaves it in WAL mode.

citations.quote: It is not possible to change the page_size after entering WAL mode
If a process sets WAL mode, then closes and reopens the database, the database will come back in WAL mode.

claims.claim_text: You have to switch back to a rollback journal mode first to change a WAL database's page size.
claims.reasoning: The passage states that a rollback journal mode is required to change the page size.

citations.quote: You must be in a rollback journal mode to change the page size.

claims.claim_text: From version 3.7.0 until 3.22.0, reading a WAL-mode database required write access.
claims.reasoning: WAL became available in 3.7.0, and the passage says older versions required write access to read a WAL-mode database, with that constraint relaxed beginning in 3.22.0.

citations.quote: Older versions of SQLite could not read a WAL-mode database that was read-only. In other words, write access was required in order to read a WAL-mode database. This constraint was relaxed beginning with SQLite version 3.22.0 (2018-01-22).
Beginning with version 3.7.0 (2010-07-21), a new "Write-Ahead Log" option (hereafter referred to as "WAL") is available.

claims.claim_text: SQLite's default page size is 4096 bytes.
claims.reasoning: The passages do not state SQLite's default page size.

claims.claim_text: Converting a database to WAL fails if the VFS does not support the necessary shared-memory primitives.
claims.reasoning: The passage gives lack of VFS support for shared-memory primitives as an example of when conversion to WAL could not be completed.

citations.quote: If the conversion to WAL could not be completed (for example, if the VFS does not support the necessary shared-memory primitives) then the journaling mode will be unchanged and the string returned from the primitive will be the prior journaling mode (for example "delete").

claims.claim_text: In that case, the journal_mode pragma returns an error.
claims.reasoning: The passage says the pragma returns a string and that on failed conversion it returns the prior journaling mode, not an error.

citations.quote: The journal_mode pragma returns a string which is the new journal mode. On success, the pragma will return the string "wal". If the conversion to WAL could not be completed (for example, if the VFS does not support the necessary shared-memory primitives) then the journaling mode will be unchanged and the string returned from the primitive will be the prior journaling mode (for example "delete").
